newsitem.title: UK: Ldn gold finds support above $340, platinum weaker.
newsitem.headline: Ldn gold finds support above $340, platinum weaker.

text.p: Sentiment in gold received a fresh blow on Wednesday after an analyst suggested that central banks could activate reserves, but the market pared its losses.
Platinum eased further in the afternoon, but prices were underpinned by protracted delays in Russian supplies.
Bullion fixed at $341.00 an ounce from $340.70 after having lost some 90 cents earlier. Spot bullion finished in London at $340.70/$341.20, down 70 cents from Tuesday's close.
"There seems to be real interest to sell gold but I think $340.00 is a relatively comfortable place for it at the moment," said one London dealer.
Others reckoned that after failing to surface above $343.00 in the last few days, gold was likely to look at support around last week's lows of $337.50 and possibly sink to $332.00.
Andy Smith, analyst at Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS), said central banks were likely to consider several ways of selling their gold reserves, although not all would wreck the price.
Sales would most likely originate from European central banks as tension builds up for qualifying for a single currency.
"People were marking prices down on the back of UBS comments," said another dealer. "The trend seems to be down anyway because the bounce from $338 (last week) was pretty poor.
But support at $335-$336 could intervene, especially because Monday's options expiry would keep interest bubbling at $340.00.
Aside from rises in U.S. stocks and the dollar, negative sentiment also spilled over from an easier platinum, which had spearheaded the precious metals rally that began last Thursday.
"There is a worry that the platinum thing is one big spoof and that it will come off," said the London dealer.
The white metal at one stage shed $4.50 to $373.00, but popped back up to $375.00 where it spent most of the session.
Although platinum has eased significantly from its high of $382.50 last week, volatility was expected to continue.
"With lease rates as high as 10 percent (for one month), I'm still bullish about it," said another dealer.
Russian central bank officials were in talks with Japanese trade houses this week about its future role as a PGM seller.

The apparent power struggle between the Russian precious metals export agency Almaz and the central bank is keeping the market in suspense. PGM exports have stalled since December and no agreement is in sight for sales to leading buyer Japan.
Palladium attracted borrowing activity, with one-month lease rates still quoted as high as 14 percent. Spot palladium pared earlier gains and finished 25 cents down at $154.00/$155.00.
